A sphinx is a mythical creature with the head of a human and the body of a lion. There are several sphinx statues in Egypt, but everyone knows this one, the biggest, which is at Giza, just outside Cairo. It's 73 metres (240 ft) long from paw to tail, and 20 metres (66 ft) high from the base to the top of the head. No-one knows for sure how old it is, but there are estimates of more than 2,500 years BC._x000A_

Looking beyond it, there is the Pyramid of Khafre (Chefren). It's 136.4 metres (448 ft) tall. It's thought to have been completed about the same time as the Sphinx. To this day it's a wonder of engineering, which must have been a colossal undertaking. Visitors can (for a fee) enter the pyramid to visit the burial chamber of the pharaoh._x000A_

A sphinx (Ancient Greek: Σφίγξ [spʰíŋks], Boeotian: Φίξ [pʰíːks], plural sphinges) is a mythical creature with the head of a human and the body of a lion._x000A_In Greek tradition, it has the head of a human, the haunches of a lion, and sometimes the wings of a bird. It is mythicised as treacherous and merciless. Those who cannot answer its riddle suffer a fate typical in such mythological stories, as they are killed and eaten by this ravenous monster.[1] This deadly version of a sphinx appears in the myth and drama of Oedipus.[2] Unlike the Greek sphinx, which was a woman, the Egyptian sphinx is typically shown as a man (an androsphinx). In addition, the Egyptian sphinx was viewed as benevolent, but having a ferocious strength similar to the malevolent Greek version and both were thought of as guardians often flanking the entrances to temples.
